title: Sophocles, Hesiod, Euripides (18 tragedies), and Aeschylus
shelf_note: A 14th-century codex (Plut. 32.2) from the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana containing plays of Sophocles, Euripides, and Aeschylus alongside Hesiod; it fits the greek-latin-classics tradition.
structure_note: The 143 printed repeats and 33 backsteps indicate manuscript foliation or marginal notations were misread as printed pagination. There is also a discrepancy between translated page counts (503 in structure vs 472 in catalog metadata), and 25 pages lack OCR.
reader_summary: This volume presents the 14th-century Laurentian manuscript of classical Greek drama by Sophocles, Euripides, and Aeschylus, alongside Hesiod. Although the scans are genuine, the transcription fails on manuscript layout, scrambling columns, duplicating text in phantom gloss tags, and garbling lines. The resulting English translation routinely invents dialogue, omits entire columns, and cannot be trusted.
book_verdict: A major primary source severely compromised by column reading order failures, phantom duplication, dropped passages, and leaked prompt markup. It is unfit to present to scholars until transcription and layout handling are overhauled.

title: Procli In Platonis Alcibiadem Commentarius (Barocci 140)
shelf_note: Proclus' Commentary on Plato's Alcibiades in Bodleian MS Barocci 140 is a late antique Neoplatonic philosophical commentary on a Platonic dialogue, belonging squarely to Greek and Latin classics.
structure_note: Page count of 336 is complete with no duplicate records. The 162 pages recorded with printed numbers reflect handwritten foliation (likely rectos only); the 7 backsteps and 8 repeats stem from OCR misidentifications of handwritten numerals rather than structural scanning defects.
reader_summary: This is a 15th-century manuscript copy (Bodleian MS Barocci 140) of Proclus' commentary on Plato's Alcibiades I. The transcription is of the correct text, but the OCR struggles with Byzantine ligatures and hand, producing non-words and substantive misreadings throughout. The English translation cannot be trusted, as it turns OCR corruptions into fabricated phrases and doctrinal distortions while leaking system XML tags into the display text.
book_verdict: Severe OCR deficiencies on Byzantine cursive Greek propagate into untrustworthy, hallucinated translations and pervasive markup leakage. This manuscript presentation is unsuitable for scholarly review.

title: Quaestiones de Primis Principiis
shelf_note: Fits greek-latin-classics: the editio princeps of Damascius' late Neoplatonic treatise Quaestiones de primis principiis, edited with Latin commentary by Joseph Kopp (1826).
structure_note: Of 424 pages, 420 have OCR and 418 are translated, with the un-transcribed pages corresponding to blank preliminary leaves or endpapers. The 14 printed backsteps and 10 repeats across 401 numbered pages reflect the transition between preliminary roman numerals and arabic pagination alongside minor leaf-numeral misreads; the volume structure is intact.
reader_summary: A reader finds Joseph Kopp's 1826 edition of Damascius's Quaestiones de primis principiis, with the Greek text transcribed accurately against the print across all reviewed pages. The English translation cannot be trusted, as it omits entire paragraphs and clauses, drops Latin commentary, and reverses key metaphysical distinctions. In addition, internal XML tags such as <summary>, <term>, and <margin> leak into the reader text throughout.
book_verdict: The volume is fit to show only with strong caveats: while the Greek transcription is nearly flawless, the English translation frequently drops text, misrepresents core philosophical arguments, and is marred by raw XML markup leaking into the reader interface.

title: Vitruvii de architectura libri X
shelf_note: A 13th-century manuscript copy of Vitruvius' De architectura from the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana firmly belongs in Greek and Latin classics.
structure_note: The 18 printed backsteps and 14 repeats across 84 pages flagged with printed numbers represent spurious OCR detection of foliation or text in a 13th-century manuscript rather than actual pagination defects, with nearly full transcription coverage (114 of 116 pages).
reader_summary: This is a 13th-century manuscript copy of Vitruvius' De architectura from the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana. Although the scans contain the genuine Latin treatise, the transcription regularly fails on medieval abbreviations, resulting in dropped passages, corrupt readings, and hallucinated Arabic script on a blank flyleaf. The English translation cannot be trusted, as it converts OCR corruptions into incoherent nonsense—such as mistranslating Socrates as a father-in-law and fir pitch as a potter—while raw XML markup leaks into the text.
book_verdict: Unfit for scholarly use due to systemic OCR failure on medieval Latin abbreviations, major translation omissions and hallucinations, and pervasive markup leaks.
